en: Of all Bukhara, the great khan,
A formidable man risen from his people,
Temir Khan pondered a plan:
Thimble mouths and camel-calf eyes,
Limpid black eyes,
Crimson dresses and slender waists,
On whom young men looked with longing—
To go and meet Semetey,
To dance before him as they approached,
He gathered a hundred maidens.
With ornamented braids and broad hips,
With beauty like the maidens of paradise,
Tall in stature, with shining eyes,
He gathered a hundred young wives.
Broad-faced orators,
Many who could devise a plan,
Orators fluent in speech,
Many of pleasing appearance,
Skillful at finding arguments,
Stout-hearted, formidable men,
Komuz players and fiddle players,
All the performers,
With sweet speech and honeyed words,
Temir Khan gathered them,
All the knowledgeable men.
Having his drum beaten,
Along the young falcon's road,
He gathered some sixty Sarts
And had them all sing songs.
The young wives and maidens he had gathered
Were a joy to anyone who saw them,
Satisfying the heart's longing to behold.
One young wife and one maiden,
He arranged them two by two,
Had swings set up,
Made a bright, red-mottled display,
With all the world's riches,
Along this boy's road,
Making a spectacle of delight.
Seeking shelter in broad Bukhara,
Your orphan entered,
Through what had been set before him,
Through those entertainments.
His splendid teeth like great doors,
The panther's hapless offspring,
Grown beyond the size of a millet seed,
Appeared like Mount Opol.
Not one person stepped forward.
When they saw the boy's appearance,
The gathered wives and countless maidens
Scattered in every direction.
His eyes blazed fiercely like fire;
Bloodlust gripped him hard.
His father Manas, the panther,
Seemed to have died this very day;
As though Manas's funeral prayer had been read,
As though he had been buried only today,
He suffered for his father,
As though feeling that bereavement only today.
In fury, the boy could not endure it;
He could not stand and think.
His rib bones seemed to come apart;
Your hapless boy's heart
Was broken into so many pieces.
The crescent axe with golden cheeks,
As though his father had departed today,
Showed at his flank.
Hearing the bald man's words in the forest,
Hearing, 'Your people are another,'
Hearing it and grieving,
He rode firmly on, heedless.
Your hapless boy, born of a champion,
Those maidens and young wives there—
He valued them not a whit.
Hearing the courageous bald man's words,
Hearing, 'Khan Manas is your father,'
He endured a day of utter darkness.
Unable to bear his grief,
The boy hurried along his road.
The lament-singer and fiddle player—
The boy did not turn aside for them.
He did not go to the entertainers;
Of those who put on the amusements,
He troubled not a single one.
Riding firmly on, heedless,
The khojas and mullahs before him—
He valued them not a whit.
In Ismayyl's plane-tree garden,
Ringed with apple branches,
At its very center was a gray mound.
Built upon that gray mound
Was a tower for watching the enemy.
To the foot of the tower,
The boy came raging and distraught.
'Temir Khan and Ismayyl
Have hidden my lineage,' he said,
Taking the deepest offense.
Akshumkar in his hand,
He sent flying toward a plane tree.
The fine white-cloth coat he wore,
He stripped off and flung upon the ground.
The boy would not relent, but raised a quarrel.
He let Aktulpar loose,
Pillowed his head upon the broad-pommeled saddle,
And lay with his head toward the qibla.
Temir Khan's Zulpukor
He laid beside his hip.
From his fierce father Manas,
The fine white-cloth coat worn as a gift,
He spread across himself from head to foot.
He did not open his closed eyes,
Did not draw back his outstretched legs,
Did not stir awake with a groan,
Did not turn to either side,
Made no movement, not the slightest,
The orphan did not move or twitch.
Persisting in protest, distraught,
He had come to the gray mound
And lay there offended.
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara—
Before Temir Khan
Many people went to bring the news.
Hearing the messenger's words,
'This orphan born of a bloodshedder
Lies there offended,' he heard.
Hearing the words of those who came,
'If he rages in boundless resentment,
This great Bukhara standing here,
He will burn it down,' he heard.
His heart was sorely troubled,
Temir Khan, khan of Bukhara.
Tears poured from his eyes;
His thoughts wandered far away.
Although he had not fathered Semetey,
He had taken him for his son.
His plump little gray-mottled falcon,
He loved him above all mortals,
That Semetey there,
His gray hawk, his morning star.
The spring of his flowing river,
His child gained after long suffering—
Temir Khan hurried in haste
To the mound where Semetey lay.
Coming up, he looked:
Pillowed on the broad-pommeled saddle,
His head turned toward the qibla,
There lay Semetey.
When he saw Semetey,
He prepared an offering to Baabedin.
Seven black bulls
He had driven out through his gate.
Displaying his ample means,
There where the bulls arrived,
He had them slaughtered and cut up.
Doing all manner of things in the open,
As every thought came to mind,
Sixty calves and forty goat wethers
He slaughtered again as an offering.
The wayward boy did not relent.
Then the boy Semetey,
The hapless boy, did not stir.
Truly created by God—
Did you see that he was His servant?
